item.title: In the Shadow Cast by Joy
item.description:
Grief

In the Shadow Cast by Joy

You don’t have to be alone in the shadow of joy.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • With media focused on heroic rescues and miracle survivals, those grieving on the sidelines can be overlooked.
  • Those who suffer can be supported while good fortune is celebrated.
  • Reaching out for support from the sidelines can be one step in the search for meaning in the midst of loss.
  • Being social is essential to being human. We celebrate together and we gather to mourn together.
Source: Krystine I. Batcho

When someone survives a disastrous event, succeeds against the odds, enjoys a seemingly miraculous recovery, or benefits in an exceptional way, joy can be spread as if from rays of sunshine. But in many cases of success or good fortune, there is also someone, often in the background, who finds it difficult to share the joy, as they have suffered failure or loss.

Side-by-side relief and grief can occur in circumstances from the ordinary to the catastrophic. Perhaps you remember the applause as an honor you had worked hard for was awarded to someone else. Maybe you stood aside as others were selected for the team or walked on stage for their diploma. Or you might have shared the sadness of another who was grieving on the sidelines, as you felt their sorrow vicariously.

In 2025, torrential rain caused the Guadalupe River to rise rapidly, resulting in deadly flash floods at Camp Mystic summer camp for girls in Hunt, Texas. Hailed as a hero, 26-year-old Coast Guard rescue swimmer Scott Ruskan coordinated the rescue of 165 people from the camp. As many parents were able to rejoice at reunions with their children, others received the shattering news that their children did not survive. Along with two counselors, 25 campers aged 8 to 10 years old died in the flood. Would the joy of the reunited lighten or deepen the grief of those who suffered the ultimate loss?

In 1963, a cave-in at a coal mine near Sheppton, Pennsylvania, trapped three workers in complete darkness 330 feet underground. For five and a half days, it was not known if the men were dead or alive until boreholes finally established contact. Two men, Henry Throne and David Fellin, were in a chamber six feet long, six feet wide, and nearly six feet high. The third miner, Louis Bova, was in a separate nearby chamber. While the world watched and waited, an innovative method and equipment provided by billionaire Howard Hughes succeeded in rescuing the two miners two weeks after the cave-in.

With congratulations from President John F. Kennedy and celebrations throughout the world, Bova, the third miner, remained entombed deep beneath the surface. The difficulty of grieving in the shadow of others’ joy can pose a lifelong challenge. Bova’s wife struggled to cope with the anguish of living in the shadow of the survivors’ joy. Eight months old at the time, Bova’s son, John, grew up with his grief-stricken mother and the spotlight of anniversaries that highlighted anew the miraculous rescue of the two who survived. Sixty years after the disaster, John reflected on his lifelong efforts to find meaning in the shadow of others’ joy. John’s attempts to feel connected with the father he had never known, to support his mother as she coped with the loss, and to establish his own meaningful path in life continued years after the media had moved on to more timely newsworthy events.

Research has found that initial levels of social support may decline significantly over time in the aftermath of traumatic events. Social support often decreases substantially long before victims or survivors have recovered emotionally from trauma and loss. One study found that 26 years following a 1990 fire that killed 159 of 482 people on board a Scandinavian passenger ferry, a substantial number of survivors and bereaved were still plagued by vivid memories of the disaster and thoughts of what might have been. High levels of anxiety and depression were found to persist nearly three decades after the disaster. As social support deteriorates over time, survivors and bereaved may stop seeking support accordingly.

Recognizing the contrast effect that can deepen grief in the shadow cast by the joy of others reminds us of the importance of caring for those on the sidelines, often suffering in silence while other voices capture more attention. Those grieving should remember that others often feel uncomfortable approaching to offer support. Those who would also benefit themselves by supporting others are often uncertain about how to extend their compassion and willingness to help. It is never too early or too late to start a conversation between those who are hurting and those who care about them.

It is possible to feel conflicting emotions at the same time. During times of sadness, it is possible to share in the happiness of others. Focusing on togetherness can help bridge the gap that would otherwise separate the hurting from those who rejoice. Just as empathy enables us to feel the emotional pain of others, it can also allow us to feel their happiness.

item.title: How to Handle the Curveballs of Conflict? Stay in the Game
item.description:
Relationships

How to Handle the Curveballs of Conflict? Stay in the Game

Don't let uncomfortable "uh-oh" moments in conversation create loneliness.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Differences, and the discomfort they cause, are part of all relationships.
  • Knowing how to handle conflict without fighting, fleeing, or freezing is the key to closeness.
  • Mindfulness helps us to wake up, pause, and consider how to proceed—together.
Source: Sneksy/iStock

I met with a couple recently who came in saying, "We're just not connecting. We've drifted apart...lost track of each other." In the first session, as they talked, I saw him deftly steer the conversation off-topic each time they encountered uncomfortable differences: She always wants to go to her sister's for Thanksgiving, but he'd rather stay home; she wants to travel; he's worried about savings. Meanwhile, she handled these moments by insisting, convincing, and dismissing. When I asked them what was going on, they both said, "We don't like conflict."

Conflict is the "uh-oh" feeling we get when we encounter differences. And we respond to this feeling by fighting, fleeing, or freezing, each of us according to our proclivities. In the example above, he's fleeing; she's fighting. Fleeing is a more obvious move away from conflict. Most of us think of fighting as synonymous with being comfortable with conflict. But in fact, insisting on winning and being right is simply another way of ending, or trying to end, the tension of uncomfortable differences. Both are trying to move away from this "uh-oh" feeling. The unwanted side effect is that they are moving away from the possibility of understanding more, building trust, and learning the skills that make these conversations possible.

In another couple, I saw the freeze response in action. On a sunny afternoon, Amy and Jack discussed a recent visit with his family. He described an interaction with her sister in which he felt the sister was being mean and aggressive. She then described the same scene, interpreting the moment as her sister energetically looking for connection. After her description, he became silent. I asked him what was going on.

Jack: "I don't have anything to say."

Me: "What’s going on inside?"

Jack: "Just all jumbled...we see this differently, so I have nothing to say."

And there you have it. An opportunity lost.

The problem is not the difference, nor even the "uh-oh" feeling. Both are ubiquitous and not optional. The problem is trying to get rid of the feeling by fleeing, fighting, or freezing—our three typical reactions to perceived danger. For these couples, getting comfortable and competent with the discomfort of conflict is going to be key to rebuilding the connection they're lonely for.

The Problem

Couples often think that differences are the problem. And indeed, in the middle of a tense moment, this can seem true. Yet, in fact, every encounter between two people involves differences. As much as we are the same, we are also infinitely different in how we perceive, process, express, and respond.

And these differences, even the small ones, are uncomfortable. We are social beings. Part of our sense of "we" is based on sameness of beliefs, values, and preferences. Even liking the same flavor of ice cream creates a sense of we! We need, and feel safe with, sameness, and we get uneasy when it's not affirmed. Differences are perceived as potential threats. We are most happy when we agree, especially in important relationships.

Our fear response and reactions happen with lightning speed and often without awareness. In a very old part of our brain, the amygdala, incoming signals are constantly being monitored for danger. The amygdala's job is safety first, and it responds in 20 milliseconds—fast, but not so accurate. For accuracy, the same signal must make its way to the cortex for complex processing. This takes about 18 to 100 milliseconds longer. This is not much more, but long enough that if we react behaviorally to the amygdala’s danger signal, we may close the door to other less fear-driven options. Just as we sometimes jump back at the sight of a sinuous shape in the grass, only to realize fractions of a second later that it's a garden hose, not a snake, we reflexively jump back from the "uh-oh" feeling of conflict.

Unchecked and repeated over time, this jumping back can lead to relationships deteriorating. Relationships and individuals need to learn and get stronger in order to thrive. Moments of difficulty are opportunities for building the strengths and understandings that bring us closer. Part of what we mean when we say we don't like conflict is that we don't like what happens when we disagree. When we jump back in fear, fight about who's right, or freeze, we walk away with a sense of failure and discouragement. We need, instead, to feel confident and successful in handling these challenging moments.

Relationships do sometimes come apart over major differences, but much more often failure to learn to respond to differences with exploration and learning causes an erosion of trust and closeness.

The Solution

What if your differences could open onto an exploration, a shared adventure of discovering more about each other and about yourself? What if you could get better at solving problems, being more creative together? What if you could become more interested and interesting, and less lonely? What if the discomfort that has you running for cover or fighting can soften and leave you free to continue conversations, maybe even share a laugh? We can learn to inhibit our automatic fear reactions to make all of this possible.

When we don't react, but instead become alert and awake to what is going on, inside of us and between the two of us, the tension often subsides. As it does, we get a chance to enjoy our ability for complex processing. We can consider what is going on and the possible responses we might make. Our full intelligence can go to work on how to stay connected as we study the problem. This is mindfulness in action.

The Possibility of Dialogue

Everything changes when we introduce the possibility of conversation aimed at exploring together: dialogue in which the goals are learning, collaboration, and improving your relationship. This conversation is quite different than the one we usually have.

When we engage with curiosity, we find that the difference that initially triggered fear is a clue, a path, to wider explorations. These explorations enrich our relationship and help us to understand each other and ourselves better. Yes, it's hard sometimes. But, as you may already suspect, this hard work is necessary for creating the relationship that you envisioned when you set your feet on this path of caring and commitment.

Getting Started

To get you started, here are a few tips:

  • Learn to observe your internal reactions during conversations.
  • Learn to identify the "uh-oh" response, that feeling of discomfort.
  • Turn this into a signal to "wake up!"
  • Learn to pause and observe as the feeling softens, then consider how to stay connected and keep talking.
  • Assume that you are both right and work together to understand how that could be true.
  • Lead with curiosity, and ask good questions.
  • Learn to look for the grain of truth in what your partner is saying.
  • Change assertions and certainties into hypotheses to be explored and tested.
  • Replace the need for resolution of differences with the goal of having better conversations.

Most Importantly

Take your loneliness for each other seriously and assume you can rebuild closeness. Imagine what it would be like if, when the two of you disagree or want different things, you stay calm and open; you encourage each other to say more; you trust yourselves to find a way forward as a team. Each difference and conflict is a chance to get closer.

item.title: 3 Telehealth Red Flags
item.description:
Online Therapy

3 Telehealth Red Flags

When social media diagnosis leads to shady telehealth platforms.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • On social media, telehealth advertisements promise quick mental health diagnosis and simple treatments.
  • This can contribute to an algorithmically flattened and consumerized form of mental health diagnosis.
  • Some telehealth companies have come under fire for their diagnosing and prescribing practices.
  • Red flags point to problematic telehealth ads and harmful social media mental health content.

A “hot” “mental glow-up” is on offer from an influencer if you click on a link—not to buy the latest beauty or self-improvement product on the TikTok Shop, but to take a short mental health quiz that may lead to a diagnosis. Videos across social media platforms portray brighter, newly productive people (initially depicted as overworked and overwhelmed) after welcoming their branded aesthetic medication package at their doorstep. The before/after trope brings to mind beauty and weight loss ads, but these ads promise to medically transform your mind.

Source: Towfiqu barbhuiya / Pexels

Telehealth ideally provides remote care to those who would have trouble accessing it otherwise. Issues of telehealth advertising on social media arise, however, when they sell oversimplified and optimizable versions of complex and serious mental health issues like depression, anxiety, or ADHD.

In recent years, telehealth companies that advertise on social media and help shape our popular understanding of mental health have made headlines, with executives being fined and arrested for unauthorized distribution of controlled substances.

A massive market opened up for these medications when restrictions on telehealth prescribing of controlled substances (including some psychiatric meds requiring careful medical oversight) were lifted near the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, when access to medical care was low and need was high.

The need for mental health care and the social media push for self-diagnosis created conditions for a perfect storm of therapy tech startups, some of which have since been alleged to treat therapists as underpaid gig workers, push employees to recklessly diagnose clients and prescribe medications with little oversight, and sell patient data, including to social media companies. Recorded patient therapy sessions are reportedly being used to train AI therapy models.

Subscription telehealth companies spend millions to advertise on social media, with mental health influencers making sponsored posts about specific diagnoses and treatments alongside their other mental health content. Celebrities are also popular spokespersons. If you have ever listened to a podcast, you are likely intimately familiar with their advertising.

It’s a tricky issue to approach because, on one hand, people engaging with mental health content for the first time may learn about and access new treatment options. This can feel powerful and life-changing.

On the other hand, a profitable industry has emerged in the partnership between social media and therapy tech that can push people toward diagnoses and treatments in ways that may be scientifically misleading and medically irresponsible.

I have compiled some red flags that can help evaluate mental health telehealth companies on social media. The presence of these indicators does not mean the company is doing something illegal or that good therapists cannot be found there. My points are meant to help critically evaluate the social media claims and point to where we should ask more questions in our mental health care, both within and outside of telehealth.

There are glaring red flags like hidden fees and platforms that are too quick to prescribe a cocktail of meds with little clinical evaluation or medical oversight. But I want to focus on broader and more insidious social media mental health discourses that can enable these kinds of practices.

The following is a partial list excerpted from my book. If promotional content (and much social media content by nature is promotional) depicts mental health and care in the following ways, we should consider whether the affiliated services can adequately address mental health suffering:

Shared singularity: The presentation of traits or symptom-based content as simultaneously universally experienced and algorithmically just “for you.” Mental health experiences of these diagnoses are highly heterogeneous—extremely complex and varied for everyone. But, as we do with astrology, we grasp onto what makes sense for us and ignore the rest; we have a bias toward making things fit, and diagnostic content is created that highlights universal experiences, which often include both an experience and its opposite (e.g., “you’re either oversensitive or don’t care at all”). Paradoxically, thousands and thousands of comments on these kinds of videos will all testify that this video is clearly just for them.

Quick fix: Traits or symptoms that are presented as easily diagnosed, treated, or optimized for personal improvement. Anyone who experiences a particular kind of suffering or struggle can benefit from one simple solution that requires very little time, money, care, support, or oversight. Not only will identifying one’s disorder lead to feeling better, but, with these treatments, it can be leveraged as a glow-up or superpower. Particularly branded diagnoses on social media (including depression, anxiety, and ADHD) often include discourses of a “high-functioning” label that is reframed as productively empowering.

Symptom-centered: Failure to acknowledge or address any external life factors that may be contributing to mental health distress; strong focus on pathology. Symptoms are presented in every case as effects of some concrete disordered condition that you have or are, and you know you have it based on your symptoms alone. Left out of the discussion is any variation of causes or the possibility that life circumstances may have contributed to suffering.

An uncomfortable problem is that oftentimes it is not just social media or tech companies presenting mental health in these limiting and potentially harmful ways. Apps and influencers leverage existing issues in mental health care, both in addressing their gaps and transplanting their flaws into platform logics and economies.

Social media breathes new life into older issues like "cosmetic pharmacology," Peter Kramer’s 1997 proposal in Listening to Prozac that psychopharmaceuticals could potentially be used for self-optimization (subsequent criticism proposed that their marketing was indeed moving in that direction). Likewise, teletherapy can exaggerate some existing problems in mental health care while trying to fix others.

This is why, when we evaluate the problems of digital mental health, it is imperative that we, at the same time, confront those pernicious issues underlying mental health models and mental health care across the board.

Excerpt reprinted from Mood Disorder: How Social Media and Therapy Tech Are Shaping Mental Health by Holly Avella, courtesy of University of California Press. Copyright 2026.

item.title: Why You Should Buy the Souvenir
item.description:
Happiness

Why You Should Buy the Souvenir

Meaningful souvenirs help us relive positive experiences long after a trip ends.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Souvenirs can serve as memory cues that reconnect us with meaningful travel experiences.
  • Research suggests sentimental souvenirs can help sustain well-being after a trip ends.
  • The best souvenirs derive their value from the experiences and stories attached to them.
  • Keeping souvenirs visible may prompt positive memories during otherwise ordinary days.

We’ve been taught a fairly persuasive rule about happiness and spending: Buy experiences, not things.

Source: Samuel Isaacs/Unsplash

Spend your money on the trip to Paris, not another handbag. Go to the concert. Take the cooking class. Book the ridiculous treehouse in Costa Rica. Research has repeatedly found that experiential purchases tend to produce more enduring happiness than material ones, in part because experiences become intertwined with our identities, strengthen social connection, and are less vulnerable to comparison with what everyone else owns.

But maybe we’ve been a little unfair to stuff… especially stuff with glittery PARIS stamped on it.

Emerging research suggests that souvenirs can do something psychologically useful: They can keep an experience alive after it has ended.

A little portal back to the trip

Source: Coleen Rivas/Unsplash

In a recent study, researchers examined whether souvenirs could sustain travelers’ well-being after they returned home. Across three studies, they found that souvenirs strongly associated with the locality of a destination—its place, people, and past—helped carry elements of the travel experience into everyday life.

The benefit wasn’t simply about owning a nice object, though. Souvenirs appeared to support well-being partly through their sentimental value and their ability to reconnect people with meaningful aspects of the trip. The trinket worked because of what it represented, not because anyone desperately needed another miniature lighthouse.

A souvenir is technically a material possession, but psychologically it may behave more like an experience.

Researchers have found that “experiential products”—physical possessions valued largely for the experiences they facilitate—generate levels of well-being similar to life experiences and greater than conventional material purchases. The souvenir just might occupy a delightful loophole in the “experiences versus things” debate: It is a thing whose primary job is to resurrect an experience and twig the memory of the Morocco market.

In defense of the fridge magnet

Source: Sunguk Kim/Unsplash

This brings us, inevitably, to fridge magnets.

A 2024 study examined what happens to souvenir magnets after vacations. Researchers interviewed magnet owners about their everyday interactions with these exceptionally unglamorous objects.

It turns out the lowly fridge magnet punches considerably above its psychological weight.

Because magnets remain visible in the home, participants encountered them repeatedly during ordinary routines. Those encounters prompted what the researchers called “post-holiday memory work”: recalling places, people, events, and emotions from trips. These recollections were usually accompanied by positive emotional responses.

The magnet didn’t just say, “I went to Barcelona”; it said, “Remember that hot afternoon in Barcelona when we had all that sangria?”

That may be the real value of a souvenir.

Human memory needs cues. Experiences that once felt vivid gradually recede as grocery lists, deadlines, laundry, and the ho-hum moments of life occupy our attention. A physical object can interrupt ordinary life and retrieve a piece of a life we might otherwise stop accessing.

Buy better souvenirs

Source: Nastya Dulhiier/Unsplash

This doesn’t mean the path to flourishing involves buying snow globes at every airport you fly through.

The research suggests that the most psychologically valuable souvenirs may be those with real sentimental meaning: something connected to a specific place, person, experience, or a meaningful story.

A handmade bowl bought from the woman who taught you to cook in Oaxaca probably has more memory-retrieval power than a generic T-shirt bought in a panicked sprint through the terminal.

Visibility may matter, too. A souvenir buried in the back of a closet has limited opportunity to jog your memory. Something incorporated into everyday life—a photograph, piece of art, ornament, magnet, mug, or strange ceramic donkey strategically positioned beside the coffeemaker—gets repeated chances to remind you that your life extends beyond whatever small stuff you might be sweating.

So yes, still prioritize experiences over accumulating possessions. But while you’re having the experience, buy the souvenir. Not because you need another thing, but because someday, standing half-awake in your kitchen on an otherwise forgettable Tuesday, that goofy little donkey may transport you somewhere wonderful.

item.title: AI and the 'Many–One' Inversion
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and the 'Many–One' Inversion

What happens when the middle of human thought becomes hidden?

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Human development moves from one mind toward an encounter with many others.
  • AI moves in the opposite direction, turning vast human plurality into a singular voice.
  • When we think with AI, some of the intellectual middle can disappear from view.
Source: Ирина Гараева/Pixabay

Today's idea is about a curiously simple relationship between human and artificial intelligence. It's almost too simple, and captures something that might align with "first principles" thinking. A human mind begins as one, a singular experience. We enter the world from a particular point of view and gradually discover that other minds exist. We do this by reading books, learning from teachers, arguing with friends, and along the way, absorbing a culture. These "vital encounters" become part of us. And the mind does it so completely that years later we may not even remember where a self-defining idea came from.

I think we can capture this rather simply.

Human: ONE ⇒ MANY

Now artificial intelligence approaches this from the opposite direction. Large language models are trained on the "voices" of millions of people and shaped by this eclectic human expression. From that plurality, AI produces something very different from what went in. AI creates a sort of inversion to deliver a singular conversational voice that is constructed out of the many. And along the way, that individual is irreversibly metabolized into the whole. This is an important distinction.

AI: MANY ⇒ ONE

I'm calling this the Many-One Inversion.

And here's a powerful and well-established phrase that helps this idea along: e pluribus unum, out of many, one. We know it as a defining element of American history—our melting pot—where a union is formed and individuality isn't lost.

AI creates a fundamentally different kind of synthesis. The human expression that shaped the system doesn't reach us as a collection of identifiable voices. We receive an answer generated from patterns, not people. Simply put, we hear one without having encountered the many.

Of course, human thought has always involved synthesis. Discovering other minds is only part of the process. We encounter varied (and contradictory) ideas, struggle in that process, and eventually leverage that to construct ourselves.

Let's unpack this a bit more. The fuller path of human thought has traditionally looked something like this.

ONE ⇒ MANY ⇒ ONE

But when we begin thinking with AI, that path changes in an important way.

ONE ⇒ [MANY] ⇒ ONE

Using brackets helps call out a distinction. The middle hasn't disappeared; it's become less visible.

Let's take this step by step. A question starts with me. I bring it to AI, where it passes through a system shaped by an unimaginable scale of human expression. What comes back may contain ideas and connections that, in many instances, I may have never thought of or perhaps even imagined. But most importantly, they arrive being synthesized into a particular response. And that response has a sense of "cognitive finality" to it. It's impossible for me to reconstruct the lineage of each and every thought that helped shape the conclusion. I knew where the idea began. The middle had become harder to see. And that forces the question: Does the middle matter?

I don't think there's anything problematic about synthesis itself. We depend on it constantly. A good professor can compress years of experience into an hour, and an editor can bring clarity to a complex argument. So far, so good.

But AI changes the process. A question can enter an LLM and return seconds later as a polished answer. Its "glibness" tells us very little about the intellectual path it took. We can wrestle with that terrain ourselves, or accept its compression without encountering the terrain at all.

I think it's easy to miss because the results can look similar. Yet the cognitive paths are different.

ONE ⇒ MANY ⇒ ONE

ONE ⇒ [MANY] ⇒ ONE

"The many" have always shaped human thought, and synthesis has always been part of thinking. What changes is our relationship to the middle. Some of the encounter and integration that once took place within the thinker can now occur before an answer ever reaches us.

The answer no longer tells us what happened in the middle. And as AI makes it so easy to stop thinking, we need to recognize that very often, the middle matters.

item.title: Can Blue Light-Producing Glasses Improve Sleep and Alertness?
item.description:
Sleep

Can Blue Light-Producing Glasses Improve Sleep and Alertness?

Just 30 minutes each morning led to better sleep and next-day work benefits.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Wearing blue light-producing glasses for 30 minutes each morning improved sleep duration and quality.
  • Better sleep was associated with greater alertness, work engagement, and job performance the following day.
  • Employees with existing sleep difficulties experienced particularly strong improvements in sleep quality.

Several years ago, my colleagues and I conducted a study examining whether blue light-blocking glasses could improve employee sleep and work performance. We found that wearing these glasses in the evening improved sleep, with benefits that extended into the following workday.

But that research left me wondering about the other half of the day. If blocking blue light in the evening improves sleep, what happens if we deliberately increase blue light exposure in the morning? Could that also improve sleep and subsequent performance at work? In a new paper, colleagues and I find that it does.

Our sleep is partially regulated by a biological process known as the circadian rhythm, an approximately 24-hour cycle that helps determine when we feel alert and when we feel sleepy. Although circadian rhythms are generated internally, they are also influenced by environmental cues, especially light. Blue wavelengths of light have particularly powerful effects on this system.

Exposure to blue light late in the evening can delay our circadian rhythms, pushing back the time when our bodies are prepared to sleep. However, exposure in the morning can have the opposite effect, shifting our circadian rhythms earlier and helping synchronize our biological clocks with the external 24-hour day. This can make it easier to fall asleep at an appropriate time later that night.

One way to obtain morning blue light exposure is to spend time outdoors in natural sunlight. That works well in sunny climates with nice weather, but what can people do in adverse conditions or when they simply don’t have time to go outside? An alternative is to use blue light-producing glasses.

What Are Blue Light-Producing Glasses?

Unlike blue light-blocking glasses, which filter incoming blue light, blue light-producing glasses actively emit blue light toward the eyes. They are lightweight wearable glasses with small light sources positioned to direct blue-turquoise light toward the wearer's eyes. The glasses are designed to be worn during ordinary morning activities, allowing people to receive controlled blue light exposure without sitting in front of a light therapy lamp or spending time outdoors.

In a new study accepted for publication in the Journal of Applied Psychology, my colleagues Kathleen Keeler, Yiming Huang, Brian Gunia, Jason Moy, and I examined whether wearing these glasses in the morning could improve sleep and subsequent outcomes at work. For this study, a manufacturer of blue light-producing glasses donated 100 pairs for our research, and our research team purchased another 100 (the manufacturer did not provide any financial support for this study). Although other devices delivering similar light exposure should produce similar benefits, we tested only one manufacturer's glasses.

Testing the Effect of Blue-Light Glasses on Work

We conducted a two-week field experiment involving 182 full-time employees at a large university in the Midwestern United States. Participants were instructed to wear blue light-producing glasses for 30 minutes shortly after waking each workday morning.

However, the glasses did not always emit the same amount of blue light. During one week, they emitted blue light at full intensity. During the other week, they emitted blue light at only 1 percent intensity, serving as our control condition. We randomly assigned participants to experience the full-intensity condition first or the control condition first. Thus, every participant experienced both conditions, allowing us to compare their outcomes across the two weeks. Participants also completed daily surveys assessing their sleep duration and quality, their alertness and cognitive depletion, and several work outcomes, including work engagement, task performance, helping coworkers, and counterproductive work behaviors.

We found that morning blue light exposure increased subsequent sleep duration by approximately 11 minutes per night and improved self-reported sleep quality by approximately 3.5 percent relative to the overall average. Although these improvements were modest, they resulted from just 30 minutes of morning light exposure, without requiring participants to substantially change their routines. This suggests that even relatively small adjustments to our daily light exposure may produce meaningful benefits.

These improvements in sleep were associated with important benefits the following day. Employees who slept longer and better subsequently experienced greater alertness. Better sleep quality was also associated with reduced cognitive depletion, meaning employees had more mental resources available to sustain effort, regulate attention, and control their behavior. Greater alertness was associated with higher work engagement and more helping behavior toward coworkers. Reduced cognitive depletion was associated with improvements in work engagement, task performance, and reductions in counterproductive work behavior.

Perhaps the most interesting finding concerns the timing of these effects. One might expect blue light-producing glasses to work like a cup of coffee, immediately increasing alertness and improving performance. However, our supplemental analyses did not find significant immediate effects on alertness, depletion, or work outcomes on the same day as exposure.

Instead, the evidence supported a more delayed process. Employees wore the glasses in the morning, slept longer and better that night, and subsequently experienced psychological benefits that were associated with improved functioning at work the following day. This makes sense given what we know about circadian rhythms. Rather than acting like a stimulant that produces an immediate boost in alertness, the glasses appear to influence sleep by helping regulate the body's internal clock.

We also explored whether certain employees benefited more than others. Employees who already experienced greater sleep difficulties showed stronger improvements in sleep quality. Younger employees also experienced larger improvements in sleep duration, with downstream benefits for work engagement and helping behavior. Age-related changes in sensitivity to light may help explain this pattern, although these exploratory findings require further research.

Implications for Sleep and Work

Our findings suggest that blue light-producing glasses may offer a way to improve sleep, particularly for people who have difficulty obtaining morning sunlight. A brief session could potentially fit into an existing morning routine, without requiring people to substantially change their schedules.

However, it is important to recognize that we did not directly compare the glasses with natural morning sunlight. We therefore cannot conclude that these devices are more effective than simply spending time outdoors after waking. For people who can easily obtain morning sunlight, that sunlight likely has an analogous and perhaps even more powerful effect.

Taken together, my earlier research on blue light-blocking glasses and our new research on blue light-producing glasses suggest that managing light exposure throughout the day may be an important way to improve sleep and work outcomes. Reducing blue light exposure in the evening and increasing it in the morning may provide complementary benefits.

More broadly, this research illustrates how interventions targeting our circadian rhythms can influence our functioning well beyond the time when those interventions occur. A brief change to our morning routine may help us sleep better that night and function more effectively at work the following day. In short, blue light in the morning may elicit more restful nights and more productive days.

item.title: Reducing Barriers to Alcohol Treatment for Executives
item.description:
Alcoholism

Reducing Barriers to Alcohol Treatment for Executives

Confidential, flexible, customized care can make seeking alcohol treatment easier.

Posted October 13, 2026

Key points
  • Fear of disclosure, stigma, and disruption often deter executives and professionals from seeking help.
  • Treatment should address both problematic drinking and the underlying factors that contribute to it.
  • Abstinence need not be the starting point; moderate drinking can be explored when clinically appropriate.
Source: Cottonbro Studio/Pexels

Many high-functioning executives and professionals recognize that their drinking habits need to change. They may often drink more than intended, rely a bit too much on alcohol to unwind and have a good time, or occasionally disappear on all-night drinking binges. Yet they remain productive at work and outwardly successful. Without any clear signs of physical dependence or withdrawal, they may not feel that their drinking rises to the level of an “addiction.” Seeking professional help may seem unwarranted for a problem they believe they should be able to manage themselves. The thought of seeking help can elicit fears about unwanted disclosure, professional repercussions, or unmanageable impositions on their time. Above all, they want to avoid being pressured to stop drinking before deciding for themselves that abstaining from alcohol is truly necessary. These concerns can influence whether they seek help at all or maintain the status quo.

Ambivalence Is a Starting Point, Not an Obstacle

People rarely enter treatment for alcohol problems certain about their drinking goals. They may be aware that drinking is adversely affecting their sleep, overall health, or valued relationships yet remain strongly attached to alcohol’s pleasurable or social benefits. Ambivalence is not necessarily denial or resistance; it reflects competing motivations. Treatment should start where the person is, without requiring a particular diagnosis, accepting the label of “alcoholic,” or committing to immediate abstinence. An essential first step is for the client and treating professional to establish a collaborative, therapeutic relationship that promotes positive change without judgment or coercion.

Making the First Contact Easier

For executives accustomed to managing problems autonomously, admitting a need for professional help can feel like defeat. A brief introductory telephone conversation can help to reduce common barriers, overcome reluctance, and determine whether a clinical assessment makes sense without pressure to continue afterward. A focused clinical assessment examines drinking patterns, consequences, medical and psychological factors, prior efforts to cut back, and personal goals. It also explores alcohol’s role: stress relief, reward, coping with anxiety or insomnia, or social drinking that escalates. Alcohol-related problems span the gamut from mild to severe and in some cases involve episodes of intensive binge drinking accompanied by cocaine use and risky sexual behavior, as described in my recent post. Importantly, individuals with seemingly similar drinking patterns may differ substantially with regard to the nature and severity of their substance use problems, their underlying psychological difficulties, and their treatment needs. These differences underscore the importance of individualized assessment and treatment rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

Confidentiality Is a Critical Concern

Executives, physicians, attorneys, and other professionals may fear disclosure to employers, colleagues, licensing boards, or clients. Such concerns can deter treatment even when disclosure is unlikely. Confidentiality policies, legal protections, and recordkeeping requirements should be explained clearly. Self-pay treatment avoids insurance claims containing diagnoses and treatment information, although required clinical recordkeeping remains. Secure telehealth offers discretion without travel or waiting-room encounters.

Individualized Treatment Rather Than a Predetermined Program

Not everyone with a drinking problem needs the same type of treatment. Some benefit from a structured intensive program; others need care tailored to their circumstances and preferences. One person may wrestle with overdrinking only in certain situations, whereas another may drink excessively during business travel or other “windows of opportunity.” Physical dependence may require medical evaluation and supervised withdrawal. These situations demand different responses. Available treatment strategies include motivational interviewing, cognitive-behavioral therapy, self-monitoring, relapse prevention, medication when appropriate, and individual or group therapy. The treatment plan should reflect clinical need and personal preferences, not a predetermined program of services.

Advantages of Treatment in a Specialized Private Practice

A private psychotherapy practice that specializes in treating substance use disorders may offer a particularly suitable and attractive setting for high-functioning executives and professionals. It can make treatment more accessible to people seeking highly personalized care and greater discretion and flexibility than a boilerplate program can provide. In a private practice, patients have direct access to the treating clinician, individualized attention, and greater scheduling flexibility. These advantages are especially valuable to patients concerned about professional exposure or reluctant to enter a standardized treatment system. A licensed mental health practitioner (e.g., psychologist, psychiatrist, or other psychotherapist) with demonstrated clinical expertise in treating substance use disorders can address not only the alcohol/drug use itself but also co-existing issues of anxiety, depression, trauma, relationship difficulties, and other emotional or psychological problems that may contribute to “self-medication” with alcohol or other substances. This integrated perspective matters because treating problematic substance use without addressing underlying factors may leave important drivers of the problem largely untouched and unresolved.

Must the Goal Be Complete Abstinence?

For many patients, abstinence versus moderation is a critical concern. Some are ready to stop whereas others want to reduce consumption, eliminate binges, or regain control. A harm-reduction approach permits these possibilities to be evaluated and treated without dictating a singular goal. For individuals with significant physical dependence, changes in drinking should be medically supervised because withdrawal can be dangerous. Moderation may be feasible with less severe problems, limited consequences, and reliable adherence to limits. Physical dependence, repeated loss of control, serious consequences, and certain medical/psychiatric conditions weigh in favor of abstinence as a better choice. Nonetheless, a professionally guided trial of reduced-risk drinking may be the most acceptable and sometimes the only way for individuals to determine through firsthand experience whether moderation is achievable and sustainable. Treatment goals can evolve in real time guided by emerging evidence and supportive feedback. Respecting an individual's preferred starting goal is neither “enabling” nor offering false reassurance about the likelihood of success. To the contrary, it provides a unique opportunity to test the feasibility of moderation within the context of an ongoing therapeutic relationship. Individuals who find moderation unattainable despite professional guidance often become more motivated to embrace abstinence as a personal choice rather than an externally imposed requirement.

What Helps Executives Succeed in Treatment?

Professional achievement does not guarantee successful behavior change. More useful are openness, willingness to examine difficult patterns, and recognition of situations that precede excessive drinking. Progress often begins with identifying thoughts, feelings, and circumstances that precede each heavy drinking episode. Exhaustion, resentment, loneliness, anxiety, or feeling entitled to a reward may be early warning signs. Recognizing them permits intervention before drinking escalates. Trust also helps patients disclose setbacks instead of concealing them.

Making Help More Approachable

Many professionals delay seeking help because they anticipate unacceptable disclosure, disruption, or commitment. Initial contact can instead begin with a confidential conversation, proceed at a manageable pace, and pursue goals that evolve with experience. Seeking help need not begin with a commitment to abstinence or enrollment in a structured program. It can begin simply with an open conversation about drinking, personal goals, and what kind of help feels right and offers a genuine opportunity for positive change.
